name: += on a string in a loop
hook: Why += on a string inside a loop quietly goes quadratic.
hook_slide: `+=` on a string in a loop *re-copies* what it already built.
hook_sub: Strings are immutable. Every `+=` builds a brand-new one.
caption: Strings are immutable in Python and JavaScript. So result += w can't extend result: it allocates a new string and copies both halves in.
Join ["a", "b", "c", "d"] that way and you copy 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = {small_bad} characters. Collect the pieces in a list and join once: {small_good}.
At {n} one-letter words it's {big_bad} copies against {big_good}. That's O(n² · L) against O(n · L).
Honesty note from the lesson: CPython and V8 often special-case += and hide this. The builder is the version whose cost you can prove.
Which one is in your codebase right now? 👇
cta: Trace the copies yourself, then meet the builder pattern.

slides.h: It looks like one step per word
p: Strings are immutable. `result += w` allocates a new string of `len(result) + len(w)` and copies both in.
Every step re-copies the whole prefix it already built.
`parts.append(w)` stores a reference, not characters. `"".join(parts)` allocates once and copies each word once.
The triangular sum again: L + 2L + … + nL. The gap only widens as n grows.
CPython and V8 both special-case `+=` on strings when the reference is private, often making it linear in practice.
Rely on that and your cost depends on interpreter internals. The builder is the version whose cost you can *prove*.
